documentation.range: Osteoglossum bicirrhosum is widely distributed in the Amazon region. The species is native to the Amazon, Rupununi, western Orinoco, and Essequibo river basins, with records from Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, French Guiana, Guyana, Peru, and Venezuela. Non-native individuals have been identified in the United States including the Florida Keys (Ferriter et al. 2008), in the Powsinkowskie Lake, an urban water reservoir located in Poland (Maciaszek and Sosnowski 2019), in Singapore (Ng and Lim 1997) and China (Xiong et al. 2015), where it is believed to have been introduced as a result of the ornamental pet trade (Crossman and Cudmore 1999).
documentation.population: This migratory fish species exhibits declines in its population linked to the fishery. Studies in the Amazonian floodplains have also demonstrated a significant negative impact on Silver Arawana populations (Freitas et al. 2013), especially in Peru and Colombia (Garcia et al. 2008, Mojica et al. 2012). The fishery has increased in the last years in Brazil, but, despite this trend, its population is believed to be stable there (ICMBio 2018).
documentation.habitats: Osteoglossum bicirrhosum is described as a relict species, and one of its distinguishing traits is the presence of a surface mouth breather. Reaching lengths of up to one metre and weight of up to five kilograms, this fish is omnivorous with a tendency to carnivory (Rodrigues et al. 2015). To supplement its limited consumption of aquatic vertebrates, it hunts terrestrial and arboreal prey in the shorelines and flooded forests (Lowry et al. 2005). Juveniles preferentially consume phytoplankton, zooplankton, and seeds (Rodrigues et al. 2015). The species is benthopelagic and is described to be sedentary in behaviour. Its migratory movements are dictated by the flood pulse; during high waters, the population is found primarily in flooded forests, and in the dry season the population returns to the rivers and marginal lakes (Tavares-Dias et al. 2014). The breeding season varies along the basin, occurring during the dry season and early rising waters in the Amazonas and Ucayali, and being restricted to the dry season in the Napo and Putumayo (Duponchelle et al. 2016). The size of maturation also varies, ranging from 43 to 75 cm for males and 46 to 72 cm SL for females (Ayala 2001, Duponchelle et al. 2016). The fecundity ranged from 93 to 360 oocytes for females of 1,300 and 2,980 g, respectively. This parameter varies along basins, although the mean of the oocytes' diameter and mass did not vary significantly (Duponchelle et al. 2016). An important behaviour of this species to consider in its management is the parental care of juveniles.
documentation.threats: One of the greatest threats to this species is the capture of juveniles from the wild and the incidental killing of adults for the pet trade. This species is particularly vulnerable to this impact because of its low fecundity, large size of maturation, and parental care (Moreau and Coomes 2006). The species is also threatened by the predatory fishery, which helped to reduce the stocks in Colombia and Peru (Garcia et al. 2008). Additionally, as a migratory species, its large range is threatened by oil and gas exploration, deforestation, and subsequent siltation of rivers and land conversion of floodplains via drainage (Costa and Carvalho Freitas 2015). Studies in Amazonian floodplains have also demonstrated a marked negative impact of drought on this species (Freitas et al. 2013).
documentation.measures: The species is assessed nationally as Vulnerable in Colombia (Mojica et al. 2012). There are currently some measures protecting this species, including a ban on commercial sale and transport of the species between September 1st and November 15th in Colombia. However, better reproductive protection is recommended, alongside regulation of the fishing and capture for the fish trade. The sale of this species for the pet trade is economically important to Peru where education of local communities to improve fishing practices would help reduce the negative impacts. Local communities in the lower Chaqueta river have altered their capture techniques to reduce impacts on the adult populations. The species is fairly well documented but would benefit from enhanced research into population, harvest, trade and habitat trends in order to manage the species more effectively in the future.
documentation.use_trade:
This species is highly commercialized in the international pet trade of juveniles. Adults are consumed through local subsistence fishing. The method of collection from the wild can destabilize the populations because, in order to collect young individuals for the pet trade, the adults usually are killed (Moreau and Coomes 2007). The collection of Osteoglossum bicirrhosum for the international pet trade provides a significant income to rural communities in Peru, where over a million individuals have exported annually (Moreau and Coomes 2006). Of the individuals taken from Colombia for the international pet trade, 93% are less than 10 cm and 7% are between 10-20 cm (Agudelo-Zamora et al. 2007). The main importer is China, where this species is highly regarded as a symbol of status, believed to bring luck, and referred to as Dragonfish. The exploitation of the species in Colombia and Peru for the pet trade has been considered controversial since it impacts this fishery resource in the Brazilian communities located downstream.

Despite the aquaculture potential (Costa et al. 2009), this species is harvested in the wild to supply local fish markets and for exportation (Lima and Prang 2008, Maldonado et al. 2017). In trying to regulate the exploitation, some countries have adopted policies to regulate their fishery at national levels (Maldonado et al. 2017), which declined the landings of the species in Peru and Colombia (Garcia et al. 2008). On the other hand, the fish landings increased in Brazil, despite its population being stable (IMCBio 2018).
documentation.rationale: The population of Osteoglossum bicirrhosum has declined in some areas of its distribution, such as Colombia and Peru, in particular due to the capture of juveniles for pet trade and the fishery for food consumption. As a results, the species is assessed nationally as Vulnerable in Colombia. However, the species seems to have a stable population trend in other countries, which represents the major distribution area of the species. Even in Brazil, where the fish landing of the species increased, this population is stable. Therefore, the species is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: There are no taxonomic limitations relevant to taxon validation.
